title: Linearization of split-torus actions on vector groups
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Groups are affine $k$-group schemes of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]; geometrically connected means connected after every field extension. Write $\mathbf G_a(R)=(R,+)$ and $\mathbf G_m(R)=R^\times$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. A represented fppf quotient means a group scheme representing the sheafification of the right-coset functor for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings of commutative $k$-algebras. An action by group automorphisms is a $k$-morphism satisfying the action identities and preserving multiplication after every commutative $k$-algebra extension. Let $d,s\geq0$, let $C$ be isomorphic as a $k$-group to $\mathbf G_a^d$, and let $E=\mathbf G_m^s$ act on $C$ by group automorphisms. There exist a $d$-dimensional $k$-vector space $W$, a group-scheme isomorphism $a:\mathbb V(W)\xrightarrow{\sim}C$, and a homomorphism $\rho:E\to\operatorname{GL}(W)$ such that $a_R(\rho_R(e)w)=e\cdot a_R(w)$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$, $e\in E(R)$ and $w\in W\otimes_kR$. Here $\mathbb V(W)(R)=(W\otimes_kR,+)$, represented in a basis by affine $d$-space, and $\operatorname{GL}(W)(R)=\operatorname{Aut}_R(W\otimes_kR)$. Equivalently the linear action is a $k$-linear coaction $c:W\to W\otimes_k k[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_s^{\pm1}]$ with $(c\otimes1)c=(1\otimes\Delta)c$ and $(1\otimes\varepsilon)c=1_W$, where $\Delta(t_j)=t_j\otimes t_j$ and $\varepsilon(t_j)=1$. Thus the assertion allows a change of additive polynomial coordinates on $C$, not only a change of basis for a previously chosen vector structure. It holds over every field and in every characteristic.

source.place: Conrad--Lichtenstein, Linear Algebraic Groups I, Appendix D.3, proof of Theorem D.3.2, printed pp.86--87, paragraph beginning Now we are in the case that U is a vector group: the positive-characteristic decomposition into a trivial-action factor and a vector factor with linear action, and the splitness of the first factor. Read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/252Page/handouts/alggroups.pdf. WANTED locally: the Conrad notes, Appendix D.3. No Stacks tag is asserted for this algebraic-group linearization theorem.

proof.text: Let $k[x_1,\ldots,x_d]$ be the polynomial ring [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] and let $P_d$ be the $k$-subspace of those $f$ with $f(X+Y)=f(X)+f(Y)$ in $k[X_1,\ldots,X_d,Y_1,\ldots,Y_d]$, an identity of polynomials, not of functions on $k$-points. Write $f=\sum_{n\geq0}f^{(n)}$ with $f^{(n)}$ homogeneous of total degree $n$ [def-pc-standard-graded-algebra]. The substitutions $x\mapsto X+Y$, $x\mapsto X$, $x\mapsto Y$ preserve total degree, so $f\in P_d$ if and only if every $f^{(n)}\in P_d$; for $n=0$ the identity reads $c=2c$, so $f^{(0)}=0$. Apply [lem-trf-additive-polynomial-monomial-classification] (with its $n$ our $d$ and its $d$ our $n$) to each nonzero $f^{(n)}$, $n>0$; its converse direction shows that the listed polynomials lie in $P_d$, and distinct monomials are linearly independent. Hence, with $\operatorname{char}k$ as in [def-pc-field-characteristic]: if $\operatorname{char}k=0$ then $P_d=\bigoplus_{i=1}^dkx_i$; if $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$ then $P_d=\bigoplus_{i=1}^d\bigoplus_{r\geq0}kx_i^{p^r}$. In the latter case let $A=k_\sigma[F]$ be the ring of finite sums $\sum_rc_rF^r$ with coefficientwise addition and $(aF^r)(bF^t)=ab^{p^r}F^{r+t}$, and let it act on $P_d$ by $c\cdot f=cf$ and $F\cdot f=f^p$. Here $f^p\in P_d$ because $g\mapsto g^p$ is a ring endomorphism of $k[X,Y]$ [def-weil-ring-frobenius], and $(aF^r)\cdot((bF^t)\cdot f)=a(bf^{p^t})^{p^r}=ab^{p^r}f^{p^{r+t}}$ gives the module law. For $a_i=\sum_rc_{ir}F^r$ one has $\sum_ia_i\cdot x_i=\sum_{i,r}c_{ir}x_i^{p^r}$, so by the direct sum $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$ is a left $A$-basis of $P_d$, and $P_d\cong A^d$. For $d=0$ all these spaces are $0$.

proof.text: If $\operatorname{char}k=0$, step 1 says $P_d$ has basis $x_1,\ldots,x_d$. Thus $\gamma(x_i)=\sum_j x_j\otimes h_{ij}$ with $h_{ij}\in H$: the action in the original coordinates is already linear over every $k$-algebra. Its matrices are invertible because acting by $e^{-1}$ is inverse to acting by $e$; the action identities give the matrix multiplication and identity laws. These Laurent-polynomial entries define a group-scheme homomorphism $\rho:E\to\operatorname{GL}(k^d)$, with $W=k^d$ and $a=b_0$. This proves the claim in characteristic zero.

source.place: Example 14.40, pp.292--293, and Proposition 14.50, p.296; agent coordinate/Frobenius-module proof of the vector-group paragraph in Conrad--Lichtenstein, Appendix D.3, proof of Theorem D.3.2, p.86.

proof.text: Define $b:\mathbf G_a^d\to\mathbf G_a^d$ by $b(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_d(x))$. It is a group homomorphism because each $f_j$ satisfies the polynomial additive identity. Both $(x_i)$ and $(f_j)$ are left $A$-bases of the same module, so write $x_i=\sum_j B_{ij}(F)f_j$. Interpret $B_{ij}(F)=\sum_r c_{ijr}F^r$ as the additive polynomial operator $z\mapsto\sum_r c_{ijr}z^{p^r}$ and define $v(z)_i=\sum_j B_{ij}(F)z_j$. Then $v\circ b=\mathrm{id}$ by these expressions. Conversely, substitution of $v$ into the expressions of $f_j$ in the $x_i$ gives $b\circ v=\mathrm{id}$: the two basis-change matrices compose to the identity, and multiplication in $A$, $(cF^r)(bF^t)=cb^{p^r}F^{r+t}$, is exactly composition of these operators. Both equalities are polynomial identities, so $b$ is a group-scheme isomorphism, with polynomial inverse $v$.
